newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan budget must impress markets, IMF.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan budget must impress markets, IMF.

text.p: When Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz rises for his budget speech on Friday, he will be seeking to convince wary lenders and investors that Pakistan is finally committed to economic reform and financial stringency.
If he fails, Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's 100-day-old government, as well as Pakistan's prospects of climbing out of its economic mess, may be doomed, analysts and diplomats say.
"Either you convince the market you are serious, or you are gone," a diplomat from a donor nation told officials recently.

The budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) is unlikely to contain any policy switches from the sweeping reforms, including deep tax and tariff cuts, already announced by Sharif's team to try to revive industry and stimulate export-led growth.
The measures were widely welcomed, but they have had little visible impact on business confidence or economic resurgence so far, with the Karachi bourse remaining in the doldrums.
"People have been waiting for the budget," said one foreign economist. "They want to see a forcible statement on where the government is going in terms of structural reforms."

The International Monetary Fund, which scrapped a standby loan to Pakistan in March, has agreed to start talks in July on a new, medium-term loan to underpin structural reforms, if end-year targets are met and the budget proves satisfactory.
The fund, stung by past experience in Pakistan, needs to be convinced that official statistics for 1996/97 provide a solid base on which to build realistic targets for next year.
Pakistan, with liquid foreign reserves of just over $1 billion, faces a critical challenge in meeting payments on its $29 billion foreign debt in the next six months.

Brokerage house KASB & Co said in a report this week that Pakistan could weather debt payments in the next quarter. "However, from September to November, payments estimated at $1.6 billion will require the government to tap international capital markets and knock on the doors of multilateral and bilateral lenders," it said. "Therefore the urgency for a budget that will convince the Fund and the markets."
In a hard-hitting report this month, the central bank urged the government to curb Pakistan's chronic fiscal deficit.
"The budget for 1997/98 should set the tone in changing the direction of fiscal management in Pakistan," it said.
Urging a drastic restructuring of the tax collection process to offset revenue losses implicit in tax and tariff cuts, the bank said the government must also clamp down on spending.
The central bank even made a veiled plea for defence spending, a heavy budget item, to come under closer scrutiny.
"Three items -- general administration, defence and interest payments -- account for the bulk of current expenditure," it said.
"There is an urgent need for a serious effort to examine all possible economies and strategic options for expenditure control in all the areas of current expenditure."
Economic indicators for 1996/97 make grim reading. "It is one of the worst years in the last few years as far as economic indicators are concerned," Aziz said on Wednesday.

An official survey said the economy would grow just 3.1 percent in 1996/97 against a targeted 6.3 percent and last year's 4.6 percent, while the budget deficit would reach 6.2 percent of GDP compared to 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
Revenue reached only 221 billion rupees ($5.45 billion) in the first 10 months, against a whole-year target of 340 billion, it said, predicting an end-year shortfall of 50 billion rupees.
Annual consumer price inflation was likely to rise 11.62 percent in 1996/97, compared to 10.3 percent last year.
The survey said the balance of payments had come under pressure because exports had grown only 1.1 percent while imports grew 1.5 percent in July-April 1996/97.
"Neglect of short-term risks relating to the budget, banking sector and external accounts could be costly, and undermine the sound long-run vision of the government," the central bank said.
